NATIONAL POLICY ON MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES (MSMEs)
Federal Republic of Nigeria
1. INTRODUCTION
Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) are the backbone of the Nigerian
economy. They account for the overwhelming majority of registered businesses in
the country, contribute close to half of national GDP, and provide the largest
share of non-farm employment. Any serious strategy for job creation, poverty
reduction and industrial growth in Nigeria must therefore begin with the MSME
sector.
This policy document sets out an agreed national framework for classifying,
supporting and regulating MSMEs. It is intended for use by government agencies,
development finance institutions, commercial banks and the enterprises
themselves.

2. CLASSIFICATION CRITERIA
The National Policy on MSMEs classifies enterprises using two criteria: the
number of persons employed and the value of assets, excluding land and
buildings.
Micro enterprise
  - Fewer than 10 employees
  - Total assets of less than NGN 10 million
Small enterprise
  - Between 10 and 49 employees
  - Total assets of NGN 10 million up to NGN 100 million
Medium enterprise
  - Between 50 and 199 employees
  - Total assets of NGN 100 million up to NGN 1 billion
Where there is a conflict between the employment criterion and the asset
criterion, the employment criterion takes precedence. For example, a business
with 15 employees but assets of only NGN 4 million is still classified as a

with 15 employees but assets of only NGN 4 million is still classified as a
small enterprise, because the number of employees is the deciding factor.
An enterprise employing 200 or more people is no longer an MSME and is treated
as a large enterprise for policy and tax purposes.

3. HOW DIFFERENT INSTITUTIONS DEFINE MSMEs
Although the National Policy provides a single official classification, several
Nigerian institutions apply their own thresholds when designing loan products
and support programmes. Students should be aware that these definitions differ.
SMEDAN (Small and Medium Enterprises Development Agency of Nigeria)
  - Micro:  fewer than 10 employees, assets below NGN 5 million
  - Small:  10 to 49 employees, assets of NGN 5 million to NGN 50 million
  - Medium: 50 to 199 employees, assets of NGN 50 million to NGN 500 million
Bank of Industry (BoI)
  - Micro:  fewer than 10 employees, annual turnover below NGN 20 million
  - Small:  10 to 49 employees, turnover of NGN 20 million to NGN 100 million

- Small:  10 to 49 employees, turnover of NGN 20 million to NGN 100 million
  - Medium: 50 to 199 employees, turnover of NGN 100 million to NGN 1 billion
Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN)
  - Micro:  fewer than 10 employees, assets below NGN 10 million
  - Small:  10 to 49 employees, assets of NGN 10 million to NGN 100 million
  - Medium: 50 to 199 employees, assets of NGN 100 million to NGN 1 billion
The employee ranges are broadly consistent across all three institutions. The
differences lie mainly in the asset and turnover thresholds. BoI is the only one
of the three that defines the micro category primarily by turnover rather than
by assets.

In practice this means the same business can be treated as micro by SMEDAN and
as small by the Bank of Industry, which affects the loan products it qualifies

4. SECTOR DISTRIBUTION OF MICRO ENTERPRISES
The national MSME survey estimated that there were approximately 36.99 million
micro enterprises operating in Nigeria. Their distribution across sectors is
heavily concentrated:
  Wholesale and retail trade      54.67 per cent
  Manufacturing                   13.21 per cent
  Agriculture                      8.92 per cent
  Services                         7.80 per cent
  Other sectors                   15.40 per cent
Wholesale and retail trade dominates the micro segment, accounting for more than
half of all micro enterprises. This concentration in trading rather than
production is one reason why the sector adds relatively little value to raw
materials and remains vulnerable to import price shocks.

5. KEY CHALLENGES FACING MSMEs IN NIGERIA
Poor access to credit
  Most micro enterprises are funded from personal savings, family contributions
  or community thrift and cooperative schemes. Commercial banks regard them as
  high risk and demand collateral that they cannot provide.
Limited market access
  Small producers struggle to reach buyers beyond their immediate locality and
  are rarely able to meet the volume or quality standards required by large
  corporate or export buyers.
Weak infrastructure
  Unreliable electricity supply, poor road networks and high logistics costs
  raise the cost of doing business substantially. Many enterprises must run
  private generators, which erodes already thin margins.

private generators, which erodes already thin margins.
Discriminatory legislation and multiple taxation
  Overlapping levies from federal, state and local authorities impose a
  disproportionate compliance burden on very small businesses.
Lack of technical and managerial skills
  Many owners have no formal training in bookkeeping, costing, marketing or
  people management, which limits the ability of the business to grow beyond
  the founder.

6. GOVERNMENT INTERVENTIONS AND SUPPORT PROGRAMMES
Government support for small enterprises in Nigeria dates back to the 1970s and
has been delivered through a long succession of agencies and schemes.
Historical schemes
  - Agricultural Credit Guarantee Scheme Fund (1977), which guaranteed bank
    lending to farmers and agro-processors
  - National Economic Reconstruction Fund (NERFUND), established to provide
    medium to long term local and foreign currency loans to small enterprises
  - Nigerian Industrial Development Bank and its successor institutions
Current institutions and schemes
  - SMEDAN, which provides capacity building, business development services,
    enterprise clusters and industrial parks
  - Bank of Industry loan schemes offering single-digit interest rates to

- Bank of Industry loan schemes offering single-digit interest rates to
    qualifying small and medium enterprises
  - Central Bank of Nigeria intervention funds, including targeted facilities
    for agriculture, manufacturing and youth entrepreneurship
  - The Finance Act 2019 and Finance Act 2020, which exempt companies with
    annual turnover below NGN 25 million from company income tax and reduce the
    rate for medium-sized companies with turnover between NGN 25 million and
    NGN 100 million
7. POLICY OBJECTIVES
The policy commits government to improving the business environment, widening
access to affordable finance, strengthening the technical and managerial
capacity of operators, and improving access to both domestic and export

capacity of operators, and improving access to both domestic and export
markets. Progress is to be measured by growth in MSME contribution to GDP, the
number of jobs created, and the share of enterprises formally registered with
the Corporate Affairs Commission.

GUIDE TO REGISTERING A BUSINESS IN NIGERIA
Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC)

WHY REGISTER

Registration with the Corporate Affairs Commission gives a business a legal
identity. Without it a business cannot open a corporate bank account, bid for
government or corporate contracts, obtain most categories of licence, or access
formal credit from banks and development finance institutions.

THE FIRST STEP: NAME RESERVATION

The first step in setting up a business in Nigeria is to reserve a business
name with the Corporate Affairs Commission. This is done through the CAC
Company Registration Portal.

The applicant proposes two possible names, in order of preference. The
Commission checks the proposed names against existing registrations and against
its list of restricted words. If a name is available and not restricted, the
Commission issues an approval notice reserving that name for the applicant.

HOW LONG A NAME RESERVATION LASTS

A business name reservation in Nigeria lasts for 60 days from the date of
approval. Within that 60-day window the applicant must complete the full
registration. If registration is not completed before the reservation expires,
the name is released and becomes available to other applicants, and a fresh
reservation and fresh fee are required.

The 60-day reservation period applies to both business names and company names.

STEPS IN THE REGISTRATION PROCESS

STEPS IN THE REGISTRATION PROCESS

Step 1  Reserve the business name on the CAC portal and obtain the approval
        notice. The reservation is valid for 60 days.

Step 2  Choose the legal structure. The main options are a Business Name for a
        sole proprietorship or partnership, a Private Company Limited by Shares
        for a company with shareholders and limited liability, and an
        Incorporated Trustees structure for non-profit organisations.

Step 3  Prepare and upload the required documents. These normally include a
        valid means of identification for each proprietor, director or trustee,
        passport photographs, the registered address of the business, and the
        proposed share capital where a company is being registered.

Step 4  Pay the prescribed filing and stamp duty fees through the portal. The
        fee depends on the structure chosen and, for companies, on the share
        capital.

Step 5  Submit the application and wait for review by the Commission. Where the
        Commission raises a query, the applicant must respond before the
        application can proceed.

Step 6  Receive the certificate of registration together with the certified
        status report, which are issued electronically.

AFTER REGISTRATION

Once the CAC certificate has been issued, the business should register with the
Federal Inland Revenue Service to obtain a Tax Identification Number, open a
corporate bank account in the registered name, and register with the relevant
state internal revenue service where it operates.

REGISTERING A CONSTRUCTION BUSINESS

A construction business follows the same CAC registration route described above.
Most construction firms register as a Private Company Limited by Shares rather
than as a Business Name, because corporate and government clients generally
require a limited liability company before awarding contracts.

In addition to CAC registration, a construction business in Nigeria typically
needs the following:

  - Registration with the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria
    (COREN) where engineering services are offered, which requires that the
    firm employ registered engineers.

- Registration with the Bureau of Public Procurement and inclusion on the
    National Database of Contractors if the firm intends to bid for federal
    government contracts.

  - Registration with the relevant state ministry of works or physical planning
    authority in each state where it intends to operate.

  - Membership of a recognised trade body such as the Federation of
    Construction Industry, which many clients treat as evidence of competence.

  - Compliance with the Employee Compensation Act through registration with the
    Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund, given the safety risks of construction
    work.

COMMON REASONS APPLICATIONS ARE REJECTED

COMMON REASONS APPLICATIONS ARE REJECTED

Applications are most often rejected because the proposed name is too similar to
an existing registered name, because the name contains a restricted word such as
"Federal", "National" or "Holdings" without the required consent, because the
identification documents uploaded are unclear or expired, or because the
registered address supplied is incomplete.
